idiom_name: guarded cell: cheap published-state test, lock-protected one-time initialiser, re-test inside the lock
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: keep exactly one cell per shared object and give it a single accessor. The accessor performs a load that carries the platform's ordering guarantee, and if the cell is still unset it takes the initialisation lock, tests again (another thread may have built the value while it waited), runs the factory, publishes through an ordered store, and only then releases the lock. The second test is what makes the lock conditional; the ordered store is what makes the whole thing correct, and it is the part that must be named explicitly (volatile, acquire/release, class-init lock, once primitive). Prefer the platform's once construct where one exists - the classic hand-written form is justified only when no primitive is available.
code_sketch:
if cell == unset:                  # fast path: one ordered load
    lock():
        if cell == unset:          # re-test: another thread may have won
            cell = build()         # publish via an ordered store
        # order matters: publish, then release
return cell                        # readers never take the lock

# where the platform has a once primitive, delete all of the above
# and call it: once(cell, build) / get_or_init(build) / lazy { build() }
pitfalls: Omitting the ordering guarantee on the publishing store: the pattern is then a data race whose symptom is a partially constructed object, not a failure at the point of the bug.
Omitting the second test inside the lock, so every caller that lost the race builds its own object and only the last one is kept.
Letting the initialiser call back into the accessor: recursive initialisation deadlocks or panics in nearly every runtime.
Holding the initialisation lock while calling out to arbitrary code, which turns the accessor into a re-entrancy hazard and can serialise unrelated work.

Using a separate boolean flag and pointer instead of the pointer itself as the publication guard: a plain bool + plain pointer is undefined behaviour in C++ and Rust, not merely a subtle memory-model issue.
Splitting the guard across two variables that can drift apart (e.g., setting the flag before the store completes, or storing to the pointer before the object is constructed).
